ending: Jonas learns that release, the community's word for removing people, is really a lethal injection, shown to him in a recording of his own father calmly killing a newborn twin. Realizing the community he obeys is built on this quiet killing and on the surrender of all real feeling, and learning that the fragile baby Gabriel is scheduled to be released, Jonas decides to act. With the Giver he plans an escape: if Jonas leaves the community, the memories he carries will flood back into the people, forcing them to feel and, the Giver hopes, to change. The Giver intends to stay behind to help them through it. Because Gabriel's release cannot wait, Jonas flees earlier than planned, taking the baby on his father's bicycle. He evades the search planes, then endures cold, hunger, and exhaustion as he travels toward Elsewhere. In the final scene, with snow falling, he climbs a long hill, finds a sled at the top, and rides down toward a valley of lit houses and the sound of music. Lowry leaves the close deliberately open: Jonas and Gabriel may have reached a real place of warmth and love, or the vision may be the last of a dying boy's memories.
in_short: Jonas lives in a tightly controlled community that has traded freedom, choice, color, and deep feeling for order and safety, a system called Sameness. At the Ceremony of Twelve he is chosen for the unique role of Receiver of Memory and is trained by an old man, the Giver, who transfers to him the memories of the whole human past, joyful and painful alike, that everyone else has been spared. As Jonas comes to know color, love, and snow, and also war and suffering, he grows disturbed by how empty and unfeeling his community really is. He discovers that 'release,' spoken of gently, is actually death by injection, applied even to imperfect babies like the newborn Gabriel his family has been minding. To save Gabriel and to force the community to feel again, Jonas flees with the baby toward Elsewhere. Cold, starving, and pursued, he reaches a snowy hill, finds a sled, and rides down toward distant lights and music, in an ending that leaves their survival uncertain.

recaps.text: Jonas, an eleven-year-old, lives in a strictly ordered community where feelings are shared every evening, dreams are told every morning, rules govern nearly every act, and language must be exact. His father is a Nurturer who cares for infants, his mother works at the Department of Justice, and his younger sister Lily is a chatterbox. Jonas is nervous about the coming Ceremony of Twelve, when the Elders will assign each child of his age a lifelong role. His father brings home a struggling newborn named Gabriel, who has the same pale eyes as Jonas, hoping extra care will help the baby thrive. Like everyone, Jonas begins taking the daily pills that suppress the first 'stirrings' of desire, and he tries to prepare himself for whatever future the community chooses for him.

At the Ceremony of Twelve, the Chief Elder assigns each child a role before the whole community. When Jonas's turn is skipped over, he is left frightened and ashamed, until the Chief Elder announces at the end that he has been selected for the rare and honored position of Receiver of Memory. He is given a list of unusual rules that set him apart from everyone else: he may lie, he is exempt from the usual courtesies, he may not discuss his training or share his dreams, and he may not ask to be released. Uneasy and isolated by this strange distinction, Jonas prepares to begin his instruction with the current Receiver, the only other person who holds the role.

Jonas begins his training with the old man he comes to call the Giver, who transmits memories to him through touch. The first memories are joyful and astonishing: sledding down a snowy hill, sunshine, and colors the community has erased in favor of 'Sameness.' Jonas starts to see color where before there was only gray, first glimpsing it in an apple and in Fiona's hair. But the Giver must also pass on memories of pain, including sunburn and, later, far worse suffering, because the Receiver has to carry the hard memories too. Jonas begins to grasp how much his community has given up, trading the fullness of human experience, its color, weather, and strong feeling, for the safety of a life without risk or difference.

As the training deepens, the Giver shares richer memories, among them the warmth of a family gathered at a holiday and the meaning of love, feelings the community no longer knows. Jonas stops taking his pills so he can keep his new capacity to feel. He grows increasingly troubled by how little the people around him truly experience, and by his own loneliness, since he cannot share what he now carries. He also bears terrible memories the Giver must unload, including the chaos and agony of war. Jonas learns that a Receiver was chosen once before, ten years earlier, a girl named Rosemary who could not endure the painful memories and asked to be released, with consequences the Giver is plainly reluctant to describe.

Jonas asks to see what 'release' truly means, and the Giver shows him a recording of Jonas's own father releasing a newborn twin: he gently gives the infant a lethal injection and disposes of the tiny body. Jonas is horrified to understand that release, spoken of as a peaceful going-away, is in fact killing, and that the community does it to the old, to rule-breakers, and to babies who do not measure up. When Jonas learns that the still-struggling Gabriel is scheduled to be released, he and the Giver make a plan: Jonas will flee the community and carry his memories away, which will force the people to receive them and to feel again. Because Gabriel's release is imminent, Jonas leaves at once, taking the baby with him into the unknown lands beyond the community.

Jonas flees on his father's bicycle with Gabriel, heading away from the only world he has known toward the distant place the community calls Elsewhere. Drawing on memories of cold to hide their body heat, he evades the search planes sent after them. The journey grows harder: their food runs out, cold rain sets in, and both boy and baby weaken from exhaustion and hunger. At last snow begins to fall, and Jonas, remembering the very first memory the Giver gave him, pushes the bicycle up a long hill. At the top he finds a sled waiting, and he and Gabriel ride down toward the bottom, where he sees the lights of houses and hears, or believes he hears, music and voices. The book ends there, leaving it uncertain whether they have reached warmth and safety or are slipping away.
